title: Early years, AI and edtech: worries, gaps and practical steps
label: 20 October 2026 · Early years evidence on AI and edtech
summary: The Committee heard from early years practitioners and researchers about rapid AI development outpacing evidence and guidance. Providers report social and emotional delays in children, widespread fear and low training for staff, and ad‑hoc use of AI mainly for administration. Witnesses urged urgent, long-term research, clearer product standards and labels, mandatory training for educators, stronger safeguards on toys and data, and careful use of AI for personalised support—while protecting human relationships that underpin early learning.

chapters.title: Frontline experience and immediate worries
chapters.takeaway: Early years managers see more children with social and emotional delays, and staff are fearful and undertrained for AI-related issues.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at AI and edtech in the early years. Could you introduce yourselves and outline the main impacts you’re seeing?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: I run the Early Years Alliance. Our members—nurseries and childminders—report more children arriving with social and emotional delays since the pandemic. Staff are dealing with aggression and stress; between January and September our 28 settings recorded 43 staff accidents, many from biting or hitting.

turns.speaker: Professor Jenny Gibson
turns.text: My research focused on AI-enabled toys that chat with under-fives. Practitioners and parents are worried. The market is changing fast and there’s almost no independent evidence on how these toys affect early language or social development.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: On the ground, people equate technology with screen time and are scared. Most nursery leaders don’t feel skilled in AI, cyber‑security or digital pedagogy, and face big staffing pressures—so technology gets avoided or used badly.

chapters.title: What tech is actually used in early years?
chapters.takeaway: Most AI/tech is used for admin or educator tools; interactive AI toys and smart speakers are turning up but frameworks and training are scarce.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What types of edtech do settings use and is there an evidence-based procurement framework?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Primarily administration and report-generation. Some products help speech and language, but many generated reports are clinical, lacking nuance. There’s no consistent framework—introduce and test later is the norm.

turns.speaker: Professor Jenny Gibson
turns.text: I’ve seen Alexa in nurseries and chatty toys. Often staff don’t know whether a device uses generative AI. Most tech is educator-facing for planning, not child-facing—yet educators don’t feel supported to judge products.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: I prefer 'digital pedagogy'—thinking about intent, implementation and impact. Non‑digital tools (sand, Play‑Doh) are also 'tech' in the broad sense. When used intentionally, tech like Bee‑Bots or wireless microscopes can support STEAM learning; but most nurseries lack training and time to experiment.

chapters.title: Safeguarding, privacy and parental pressures
chapters.takeaway: There are real risks from data, images and AI advice; parents and educators need support, and current protections are thin.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What are the specific safeguarding risks to children from AI and edtech?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Biggest risks happen at home: families under pressure use more tech. Educators often lack the training to advise parents. We need emotional safeguarding, not just physical—staff are trusted by families and should be supported to help parents use tech safely.

turns.speaker: Professor Jenny Gibson
turns.text: Toys with generative AI can encourage overly flattering, friendship‑like interaction. If children confide to a toy, that raises privacy and safeguarding questions: who sees that information and how should staff respond?

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Smart speakers are a big concern—recording devices in rooms. Nurseries sometimes put them in without policies. Also parents post child photos on social media; nurseries are cropping faces or sharing hands-only because of misuse risks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are settings following safe procurement?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Not reliably. When we do use tech we pick trusted brands and vet them, but that’s not systematic. We need product standards and accountability for manufacturers—like product safety tests for psychological harms.

chapters.title: Evidence gaps, research and regulation
chapters.takeaway: AI is developing faster than research; witnesses called for long-term studies, procurement standards, and cross‑government coordination.

turns.speaker: Mark Sewards
turns.text: Should the Government take a precautionary approach and what safeguards are needed?

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: We lack long-term, longitudinal research. Short trials don’t capture lifetime effects. The Government must coordinate across departments, fund generational studies, and create procurement standards so schools aren’t swamped by commercial claims.

turns.speaker: Meg Moss
turns.text: Risk stratification is needed: products that touch emotions or offer therapy are high risk and need stronger safeguards. Regulation helps, but public awareness and education are also critical.

turns.speaker: Dr Mhairi Aitken
turns.text: Avoid hype-driven adoption. Start by identifying real problems schools face—then assess whether AI is the right tool. Many commercial AI solutions aren’t designed with children’s development in mind.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How quickly would the research take?

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: To see meaningful developmental effects we need studies across primary and secondary years—years, not months. Policy must fund longer-term cohorts, not tiny short pilots.

chapters.title: Opportunities, SEND and personalised support
chapters.takeaway: AI can help with profiling and assistive tech, but evidence is limited, and teacher judgment must remain central to avoid bias and low-quality substitutes.

turns.speaker: Mark Sewards
turns.text: Can AI close gaps for children with SEND or EAL?

turns.speaker: Professor Jenny Gibson
turns.text: There’s optimism for profiling and targeting needs, but lots of hype and little solid evidence. Products must be co-designed with parents and children with SEND and rigorously trialled.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: I saw some promising demo tech abroad that adapts tasks to a child’s level. But policy and school priorities drive inclusion more than edtech alone.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Practical example: a tablet for a child with mobility or communication needs transformed his nursery engagement. That’s assistive tech—different from AI toys. It shows real benefit when professionals, therapists and managers work together.

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: Beware of locking schools into subscriptions for specific SEND products without evaluation. That can create a ceiling on learning and reinforce bias—assume needs, don’t personalise well.

chapters.title: Teachers, curriculum and social development
chapters.takeaway: AI should support teachers, not replace human interaction—social skills, oracy and perseverance are crucial and may be harmed if children rely on AI shortcuts.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: How should the curriculum adapt so pupils develop critical thinking and independent skills in an AI world?

turns.speaker: Professor Sarah-Jayne Blakemore
turns.text: Children’s brains are highly plastic; they need real social interaction to build social cognition. Oracy, teamwork and arguing a point are skills that must be practised with people, not just AI bots.

turns.speaker: Dr Mhairi Aitken
turns.text: We need 'critical AI literacy'—teaching young people how AI works, its limits, how to judge sources and spot AI‑generated misinformation. Otherwise shortcuts become harmful.

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: AI can be a tireless tutor that extends learning, but only if teachers are trained to use it and the curriculum builds dialogic skills. Otherwise the benefits are uneven and commercially driven.

turns.speaker: Meg Moss
turns.text: Don’t forget relational learning. Perseverance and repair in relationships—working through disagreement—are formative. Therapeutic or relational AI tools are especially risky because they can undercut real-world practice of these skills.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: How will teachers cope when students use AI to produce coursework?

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: This is already happening. The response should be twofold: adapt assessment (fewer high‑stakes copyable tasks) and teach students the skills—argument, oracy, reasoning—that AI cannot fully replicate.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final practical asks for the Government?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Fund training for educators, integrate AI understanding into formal qualifications, and give nurseries resources to advise parents—early years staff are front-line family support and need backing.

turns.speaker: Professor Jenny Gibson
turns.text: Introduce product safety standards that consider psychological risks for young children, and support cross‑sector work between health, social care and education.

turns.speaker: Professor Sandra Leaton Gray
turns.text: Commission long-term, independent research, fix interdepartmental coordination, and set procurement standards so schools are not prey to marketing claims.

turns.speaker: Dr Mhairi Aitken
turns.text: Regulate where risk is high, start from education’s needs not tech hype, and protect children’s data and privacy in any roll‑out.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Prioritise CPD and practical, hands-on time for staff to learn digital pedagogy; help nurseries move from fear to purposeful use.

turns.speaker: Meg Moss
turns.text: Risk‑stratify AI uses, urgently address therapeutic/relational AI as high risk, and look internationally for co‑ordinated standards and badging schemes.

turns.speaker: Professor Sarah-Jayne Blakemore
turns.text: Protect opportunities for children to talk, play, and build friendships—human interaction is the bedrock of healthy development.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please write to the Committee if you have further evidence; the session is closed.
